title: Terminal commands are interpreted as consisting of a command, options, arguments, and output.
body: A terminal is a window where developers issue text-based commands to a computer. What matters is not the black window itself, but the ability to understand the structure of the commands.
when_to_show: When reading terminal commands, the CLI, and execution logs
detail: For example, a command like `python script.py --check data.json` can be broken down into the program to be executed, the file being passed, the options, and the output. The command specifies what to run, the options modify how it runs, and the arguments pass target files or values. Just like reading code, commands are read from left to right. First, check if the first word is the actual program to be executed; next, see if there are any options; and finally, check which file or folder is the target.

title: Shell is a set of rules for interpreting commands, and PowerShell and Bash have different syntaxes.
body: A shell is a program that interprets commands entered by the user and passes them to the operating system. PowerShell, Bash, and zsh are all shells, but they differ in syntax and basic tools.
when_to_show: When Looking at Differences Between PowerShell and Bash Commands, Line Breaks, and Path Notation Issues
detail: PowerShell is commonly used on Windows, while Bash is frequently used on Ubuntu or Linux servers. Even within the same Python project, the line-breaking conventions, environment variable notation, path separators, and script activation commands vary depending on which shell is used to execute the commands. When reading PowerShell commands, look for verbs such as Set-Location, Get-Content, Test-Path, and Remove-Item. When reading Bash commands, short commands like `cd`, `ls`, `cat`, `grep`, `rm`, and `chmod` frequently appear.

title: Ubuntu and Linux are the foundation for server development commands.
body: Linux is a family of operating systems, and Ubuntu is a distribution that packages Linux in a user-friendly way.
when_to_show: When reading about Ubuntu/Linux server commands, WSL, and GPU server setup
detail: Even if developers work on a local Windows machine, they frequently encounter Ubuntu commands on servers, in Docker, on GitHub Actions, and on GPU workstations. Learning Ubuntu does not mean delving deeply into every operating system; rather, it means mastering the basic workflow of finding files on a server, installing packages, checking permissions, and running Python. When reading Ubuntu documentation, you’ll encounter terms such as bash commands, apt installation, sudo permissions, home directories, root directories, and file permissions.

title: When dealing with path issues, you need to consider both the current working directory and the absolute/relative paths.
body: A path is an address that specifies the location of a file or folder. In a development environment, many errors are caused by differences in the execution location rather than by the code itself.
when_to_show: When encountering FileNotFoundError, relative paths, and Set-Location issues
detail: An absolute path specifies the full location starting from the drive or root, while a relative path is determined relative to the current working directory. A path like `.\data\file.json` can point to different files depending on where PowerShell is currently located. When reading a command, first check the current working directory. In PowerShell, `Get-Location` displays the current location, while in Bash, `pwd` does the same.

title: Although `sudo` runs commands with administrative privileges, using it out of habit can be dangerous.
body: sudo is a tool in Ubuntu/Linux that allows you to run commands with administrative privileges. Since regular users cannot freely modify system-wide settings or protected folders, sudo is used only for necessary tasks.
when_to_show: When you see "sudo," "Permission denied," or commands requiring administrator privileges
detail: For example, installing system packages, restarting services, or modifying specific protected paths may require sudo. However, because of its powerful capabilities, using it incorrectly can corrupt system files or cause ownership issues in project folders. When you run a `sudo` command, it first asks why administrator privileges are needed. While `sudo apt install` is natural since it installs software on the system, you should exercise caution with commands like `sudo python script.py` or `sudo pip install`.

title: apt and pip are used for different types of installations.
body: Although apt and pip both appear to be installation tools, they serve different purposes. apt is a tool for installing Ubuntu system packages, while pip is a tool for installing Python packages.
when_to_show: When comparing `apt install` and `pip install`
detail: For example, if `import requests` fails in your Python code, you may need to run `pip install requests`. Conversely, if external executable tools such as `pdfimages`, `tesseract`, or `poppler` are missing, you may need to install system packages using `apt install`. When reading a command, first determine whether you are trying to install a Python import target or an operating system executable. `pip install -r requirements.txt` is a command to install a list of Python packages, while `sudo apt install poppler-utils` is a command to install an external tool on Ubuntu.

title: chmod and file permissions determine who can read and execute a file
body: chmod is a command used to change file permissions in Linux/Ubuntu. File permissions determine who can read, write, or execute a file.
when_to_show: When you see "chmod +x," "execution permission," or "Permission denied"
detail: If you have a script file and receive a “Permission denied” error when trying to run it, you may not have execute permissions. In such cases, you can add execute permissions using a command like `chmod +x script.sh`. Since file permissions represent a balance between security and convenience, granting them indiscriminately can be risky. When checking permissions, look at the user, group, and others categories.

title: venv is a Python toolbox used separately for each project.
body: venv does not copy the operating system; it isolates a project-specific Python path and site-packages. Activation is a PATH convenience, and an explicit environment interpreter works without it.
when_to_show: When reviewing venv, virtual_environment, python, dependency
detail: Pins and tests are also needed for stronger reproducibility.

title: "activate" and "deactivate" change which Python environment the current terminal is using.
body: Activation changes the current shell's PATH so the environment's Python is preferred; deactivation reverses that change. Activation is optional because the environment interpreter can be invoked directly.
when_to_show: When looking at the commands to activate/deactivate a venv
detail: Verify the real path with sys.executable and python -m pip --version rather than trusting only the prompt label.

title: `python -m pip` ensures that the pip currently associated with Python is used.
body: "python -m pip" means to run the pip module using the currently running Python. If you simply use "pip install," which version of pip is used may depend on the PATH settings in your shell.
when_to_show: When imports fail due to differences between the pip and Python environments
detail: In particular, if you have multiple Python installations on Windows, or if you repeatedly activate and deactivate venv, pip and Python may point to different environments. In this case, using a command like `python -m pip install requests` ensures that pip from the same environment as the current Python is used. When interpreting the command, the installation location is checked before the target to be installed. `python -m pip --version` shows not only the pip version but also which Python path pip is linked to.

title: requirements.txt is a list of packages needed to reproduce the new environment.
body: requirements.txt supplies package requirements to pip. Version ranges, a different Python or OS, and changing transitive dependencies can produce different environments, so the file alone is not a perfect lock.
when_to_show: When looking at the requirements, pip freeze, and the reproducible environment
detail: Install into a clean environment, document runtime constraints, and run real tests.

title: When encountering a `ModuleNotFoundError`, you should first suspect a mismatch in the current environment rather than whether the module is installed.
body: ModuleNotFoundError means Python could not resolve an import name. Causes include an environment mismatch, a typo, launch location, package structure, or a local file shadowing another module.
when_to_show: When you encounter import errors or package installation issues
detail: Check sys.executable, python -m pip show, the import path, and filenames in order.

title: Git manages the working directory, staging area, commits, and remote repositories separately.
body: Git is a tool for managing the history of file changes.
when_to_show: When looking at the overall Git workflow and the relationship between status, add, commit, and push
detail: Beginners often think of Git as something like a "Save" button, but in reality, it consists of distinct components: the working directory, the staging area, commits, and remote repositories. The working directory contains the current state of the files you’re editing, while the staging area is where you select changes to include in your next commit. A commit is the action of saving the selected changes as a single record, and “remote” refers to a remote repository like GitHub. When reading Git commands, you should check which stage your changes are currently in.

title: "status," "diff," "add," and "commit" are the basic steps for safely creating a commit.
body: `status`, `diff`, `add`, and `commit` are Git’s most basic workflows. `git status` shows which files have changed, and `git diff` shows exactly which lines have been added or deleted.
when_to_show: When reviewing git_status, git_diff, git_add, git_commit
detail: `git add` selects the changes to include in the next commit, and `git commit` saves that set of changes as a commit. Following this sequence helps minimize the risk of accidentally committing temporary files or unintended changes. After modifying the code, first run a validation command, then use `git status --short` to view the list of modified files. After confirming that only the expected files have been modified, use `git diff --stat` to assess the scope of the changes, and check the file-by-file diff if necessary.

title: "tag," "push," and "pull" are commands used to synchronize the local repository with a remote reference.
body: A tag is a label attached to a specific commit. If you apply a tag when a feature has stabilized or at a deployment milestone, it makes it easy to revisit that state later.
when_to_show: When viewing tag creation, the origin/main branch, and the push/pull workflow
detail: `push` is a command that sends local commits or tags to a remote repository, while `pull` is a command that fetches remote changes and merges them into the local repository. `origin` is typically the default remote repository name, and `origin/main` refers to the state of the remote `main` branch. When reading commands, you must distinguish whether a commit exists only locally or has also been pushed to the remote repository. Even after running `git commit`, the changes are not yet reflected on GitHub.

title: "branch," "conflict," and "restore" are ways to split and revert changes.
body: A branch is a Git feature that creates a separate workflow from the main branch. Major experiments or risky changes can be carried out on a new branch and merged into the main branch after validation.
when_to_show: When viewing branches, merge conflicts, and undo commands
detail: A merge is the action of combining changes from another branch into the current branch. If different people have made conflicting changes to the same part of the same file, a conflict occurs. Since Git cannot automatically resolve this, a user must review the conflict indicators and choose which changes to keep. Undo commands have different scopes.

title: Environment variables and .env files inject configurations and secrets from outside the code.
body: Environment variables are configuration values injected from outside the code.
when_to_show: When viewing API keys, .env, os.getenv, and environment settings
detail: It is safer not to hardcode values that vary by environment—such as API keys, database addresses, execution modes, and model paths—directly into the code. A .env file is used to store these values separately during local development, and Python code can read them using `os.getenv` or the `dotenv` library. It is crucial not to upload actual sensitive values to public repositories. When reviewing code, trace where configuration values come from.

title: GPU, NVIDIA driver, CUDA, and PyTorch CUDA build are different layers.
body: Separate GPU hardware, the NVIDIA driver, the PyTorch build in the selected environment, and its compatible CUDA runtime.
when_to_show: When looking at CUDA installation, GPU servers, and the PyTorch runtime environment
detail: PyTorch wheels can bundle required runtime components, so a system CUDA toolkit is not always required. Compare nvidia-smi, torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.version.cuda, and sys.executable.

title: `torch.cuda.is_available` checks whether PyTorch can actually use the GPU.
body: `torch.cuda.is_available()` is a function that checks whether PyTorch in the current Python environment can use a CUDA GPU.
when_to_show: When looking at the code for checking PyTorch CUDA and selecting a device
detail: If this value is `True`, it means that PyTorch can use a CUDA device; if it is `False`, the code will run on the CPU, or you will need to review your environment settings. In AI code, it is common to use a pattern like `device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'` to use the GPU if available, and fall back to the CPU if not. When reading code, verify that the model and tensors are on the same device. `model.to(device)` moves the model parameters to the CPU or GPU, while `tensor.to(device)` moves the input data to the same device.

title: nvidia-smi is a basic diagnostic tool for checking GPU usage and VRAM status.
body: `nvidia-smi` is the primary command for checking the status of an NVIDIA GPU. This command displays the GPU name, driver version, CUDA compatibility information, GPU utilization, VRAM usage, and running processes.
when_to_show: When you see "GPU usage," "VRAM shortage," or "CUDA out of memory"
detail: When AI tasks are running slowly, you can quickly check whether the GPU is actually being used, if memory is already full, or if another process is monopolizing the GPU. When reviewing the output, look at the “GPU util” and “memory usage” metrics. A low “GPU util” value does not necessarily mean the GPU is performing poorly. The GPU may be waiting due to data loading, CPU preprocessing, or disk I/O.

title: A virtual environment is a project-specific Python toolbox.
body: A virtual environment is not a way to install Python anew, but rather a method for isolating the package space used by a single project. For example, Project A can use NumPy 1.x, while Project B can use NumPy 2.x. If you mix the two in a single global environment, it becomes confusing later on to determine which project depends on which version. That’s why you typically create a .venv file inside the project folder and activate it only within that terminal. The key is to isolate “the Python environment used by this project,” rather than “the Python environment for the entire computer.”
detail: It’s easy to think of a virtual environment as a project-specific Python toolbox. Rather than changing the Python installation on the entire computer, it isolates a separate space for the packages used by a specific project. This helps reduce conflicts when multiple projects require different library versions and makes it easy to recreate the same environment later.

title: The reason for using a virtual environment is to reduce conflicts and ensure reproducibility.
body: The main reason for using a virtual environment is to minimize package conflicts, since the required libraries and versions can vary from project to project. Another reason is reproducibility. If you save the environment you’ve created in a `requirements.txt` file, you can recreate a similar environment later on another PC or server. As a beginner, you might wonder, “Why make things so complicated?” but as soon as you have two or more projects, a virtual environment becomes a safety net that helps reduce mistakes.
detail: The reason for using a virtual environment is to minimize package conflicts and ensure a reproducible runtime environment. While this may seem like a hassle when you’re working on a single project, as the number of projects increases, it becomes difficult to trace which global installation caused a code failure. When used in conjunction with `requirements.txt`, it makes it easy to recreate the environment on a new PC or server.

title: You must use pip after running `activate` for the installation to take effect in that environment.
body: Activation makes python prefer the environment interpreter, which is convenient for installation and execution. It is not required; the environment's Python can be invoked directly. Use python -m pip and sys.executable to confirm that installation and execution target the same interpreter.

title: requirements.txt is a notepad for recreating the installation list.
body: requirements.txt is a list of packages required for a project. Typically, you can generate it by running `pip freeze > requirements.txt` to save the list of installed packages in the current environment, or you can manually list only the essential packages. On another computer, you can recreate a similar environment by running `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`. It’s important to note that while `requirements.txt` isn’t code itself, it serves as a checklist of what’s needed to run the code. That’s why it’s often included alongside the code when uploading it to GitHub.
detail: requirements.txt is a file that lists the packages required to run the project. Although it is not code itself, it serves as a checklist for setting up the environment to run the code, so it is often included in the repository. In a new environment, run `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt` to install the packages. Don’t just check for a successful installation message; you must also verify that the code actually runs.

title: Ubuntu and WSL can serve as a way to practice Linux commands.
body: Ubuntu is a Linux distribution that frequently appears in documentation on server development and AI development. WSL is a feature that allows you to run a Linux environment within Windows. In Windows, you often use PowerShell commands, while in Ubuntu/WSL, you typically use bash commands. Even for a simple task like navigating to a different folder, the syntax differs—PowerShell uses `Set-Location`, while bash uses `cd`. Therefore, when reviewing commands, you should first check which shell you are currently using.
detail: Ubuntu is a Linux distribution frequently mentioned in server development documentation, and WSL is a feature that allows you to practice using a Linux environment within Windows. Since PowerShell and Bash have different command syntaxes, you must verify which environment a copied command is intended for. It’s important to get into the habit of checking your current shell and path notation first.

title: sudo requests administrator privileges, but it is not a one-size-fits-all solution.
body: In Linux, `sudo` means to run a command with administrative privileges. It may be necessary when installing system packages, such as with `apt install`. However, it’s risky to always use `sudo` just because you get a “Permission denied” error. This is because the issue could stem from an incorrect file path, a faulty virtual environment, or a lack of execution permissions. In particular, habitually using `sudo` with `pip install` can cause packages to get mixed in with the system Python, which can lead to further complications with your environment later on.
detail: "sudo" means running a command with administrative privileges; it is not a magic button that fixes every error. If you see a "Permission denied" error, you should first check the file location, execution permissions, ownership, and any issues with the virtual environment. In particular, be careful when using `sudo pip install`, as it can mess up your system Python.

title: To troubleshoot CUDA issues, check the GPU, drivers, and PyTorch build separately
body: When a GPU isn’t detected during AI development, don’t focus on just one possible cause. First, use `nvidia-smi` to verify that the GPU and drivers are recognized. Next, check in PyTorch to see if `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns `True`. Even if a GPU is present, you may not be able to use it in your Python code if the drivers, CUDA runtime, or PyTorch CUDA build are incompatible. A “CUDA out of memory” error is often caused by insufficient VRAM rather than an installation issue, so the recommended approach is to reduce the batch size.
detail: If you encounter a CUDA issue, you should check the GPU hardware, NVIDIA driver, CUDA runtime, and PyTorch CUDA build separately. While `nvidia-smi` displays the hardware and driver status, you must use `torch.cuda.is_available` to verify whether your Python code is actually using the GPU. An OOM error is more likely caused by insufficient VRAM than by an installation issue.

title: Start by learning the Git workflow: status → add → commit → push
body: When you’re first learning Git, you don’t need to memorize all the commands at once. Start by using `git status` to check your current changes, then use `git add` to select the files you want to include in the commit, and finally use `git commit` to create a local commit. To push changes to a remote repository like GitHub, use `git push`. `git diff` is a command that lets you check what has changed before committing. The key point is that “modifying files,” “committing changes,” and “pushing to a remote repository” are distinct steps.
detail: The basic Git workflow involves checking the status to review changes, using `add` to select files to commit, creating a local commit with `commit`, and then pushing the changes to the remote repository with `push`. Modifying files, saving changes, and pushing them to the remote repository are distinct steps. Checking the diff before committing can help minimize unintended changes.
